title: Estimating the cost of training disruptions on marathon performance
authors: Feely C, Smyth B, Caulfield B, Lawlor A
journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
population: Recreational runners who completed marathons in 2014-2017; more than 15 million activities from 300,000 runners; cost estimated in runners with both a disrupted (>=7 days) and an undisrupted marathon
findings: A disruption was a complete cessation of training within the 16 weeks before the marathon; over 50% of runners had short disruptions of up to 6 days, and longer disruptions were increasingly less frequent among those who reached race day.
Runners with a disruption of 7 days or more had a finish-time cost of 5-8% versus their own marathon with only short (<7 day) disruptions.

Likelihood of disruption differed little (<5%) by sex, age, ability and timing, but the cost differed more (10-15%): males 5% vs females 3.5%; faster runners 5.4% vs slower 2.6%; late disruptions 5.2% vs early 4.4%.
Group differences were tested with two-sample t-tests.
limitations: Within-runner comparison, but only runners who reached race day (survivorship); cause of disruption unknown (illness, injury, life); self-selected tracker data; the cost comparison uses the subset with multiple marathons, not all 300,000; no confidence intervals in the abstract. Crossref gives 2023-01-10 online, Europe PMC year 2022 (volume 4).
implications: Count a full-rest gap of 7 or more days in the 16 weeks before a race as a strong negative signal (about 5-8% slower projected finish); tolerate gaps under 7 days.
After a 7+ day gap, re-plan remaining weeks with a graded restart and widen or slow the goal-time projection; protect the final weeks from planned breaks since late gaps cost more (5.2% vs 4.4%).
Schedule to avoid 7 days without running; present targets as adjustable sketches.

verification.notes: Crossref title, journal, first author match; issued year 2023 vs Europe PMC 2022, 2022 kept (volume year). Abstract re-fetched; all percentages match.
